sermon:
## How Lonely Sits the City
*A widow in the rubble, and the only face she can still bear to turn toward*

**Text:** Lamentations 1 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 9:1; Psalm 137:1; Isaiah 1:21; Matthew 23:37

The book of the Bible that the church reads least is the book that the grieving reader needs most. Lamentations does not open with an answer. It opens with a woman sitting in the ashes of a burned city, and the first word out of her mouth is not a confession and not a doctrine. It is a sob.

**The city that has nobody left to comfort her**
The poet does not begin with God. He begins with a street. "How lonely sits the city that was full of people. How like a widow has she become, she who was great among the nations." (Lamentations 1:1) Jerusalem is not described from the height of a watchtower. She is described from the ground, the way you would describe a friend you found weeping after the funeral. Once full. Now empty. Once a princess among the provinces. Now under tribute. The grief is specific, and the specificity is the mercy, because grief abstracted is grief dismissed. The poet refuses to round the suffering up into a lesson. He counts it. "She weeps bitterly in the night, with tears on her cheeks. Among all her lovers she has none to comfort her." (Lamentations 1:2) Five times in this chapter the same wound is pressed. She has no comforter. Not one. The exiles by the rivers of Babylon knew this silence, sitting down and weeping when they remembered Zion (Psalm 137:1). Jeremiah knew it, wishing his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, that he might weep day and night for the slain of his people (Jeremiah 9:1). The man who saw it coming did not gloat when it came. He wept.

Notice what the poet refuses to do. He does not hurry. The first eleven verses circle the same ground, the loneliness, the betrayal of the lovers, the roads that mourn because no one comes to the appointed feasts, the priests who groan, the young women who grieve. He lingers in the wreckage like a man who knows that grief skipped over is grief that festers. There is no impulse here to fix, to apply, to land the lesson and move on. He sits down in the loneliness and stays there, verse after verse, and that staying is the first thing this book teaches a church that has forgotten how to weep.

**Grief that will not lie about its own cause**
Here is where Lamentations refuses to be a self-help book. The poet will not let the widow pretend she is only a victim. Halfway through the chapter the voice turns, and the city speaks for herself, and what she says is unbearable in its honesty. "The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word." (Lamentations 1:18) She does not say the disaster was random. She does not say it was unfair. Isaiah had named the slide a century before — the faithful city become a whore, justice once lodged in her, now murderers (Isaiah 1:21). The grief here is not the clean grief of the innocent. It is the harder grief, the grief that is tangled up in your own sin, the grief where you cannot separate what was done to you from what you did. And the poet will not separate them for her, because that separation would be a lie, and a lie is no comfort. Not innocent suffering. Guilty suffering, fully owned. This is the grief most of us actually carry, and it is the grief the church is worst at sitting with, because it does not resolve into a tidy verdict about whose fault it was. It was hers. And she is still allowed to weep.

This is the second thing the church gets wrong about lament. We think confession ends the crying — that once you have admitted your fault, you forfeit your tears, because now the suffering is deserved and tears over a deserved thing feel like self-pity. The poet does not believe that. He puts the confession and the weeping in the same mouth, in the same chapter, in the same breath. "For these things I weep. My eyes flow with tears, for a comforter is far from me." (Lamentations 1:16) She owns the rebellion and she keeps the tears, and Scripture does not correct her for it. The deserved disaster is still a disaster. The guilty griever is still a griever.

**The one face she can still turn toward**
So what does a guilty griever do when there is no comforter on earth and the ruin is partly her own doing. She does the one thing that has any future in it. She turns her face back toward the God who is in the right and asks him to look. "Look, O LORD, and see, for I am despised." (Lamentations 1:11) "See, O LORD, my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed." (Lamentations 1:9) She does not demand acquittal. She asks to be seen. And this is the hinge the whole book turns on, the thin thread that keeps lament from collapsing into despair — she still believes the God who struck her is the God who sees her, and she would rather be seen by him in her ruin than comforted by anyone else in a lie. I have done the opposite. I have run from the only face that could hold me, because that face had also disciplined me, and I called the running self-protection. We do this. We treat the God who wounded us as the one person we cannot go back to, when he is the only one we can. There is a city in the gospels, and a man weeping over it. "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not." (Matthew 23:37) The widow with no comforter has a comforter. He is standing on the hill looking at the same ruined city, and he is crying. He came to be the man of sorrows so that the woman of sorrows would have someone in the ashes with her. The cross is God refusing to comfort us from a safe distance.

Look on my affliction, LORD.

## The LORD Has Become Like an Enemy
*The night you cannot explain away, and the God you cannot let go of*

**Text:** Lamentations 2 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 63:10; Job 16:12; Jeremiah 30:14; Hebrews 12:6

There is a sentence in this poem that most of our worship songs are built to keep us from ever saying. The poet says it anyway. He says it because it is true, and because a faith that cannot say the true thing is not a faith, it is a managed performance.

**The hand we do not want to name**
We are comfortable saying the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem. We are comfortable saying the people sinned. What the second poem does is take both of those true things and reach past them to a harder one. "The Lord has become like an enemy. He has swallowed up Israel." (Lamentations 2:5) Not Babylon swallowed Israel. The Lord did. The poet stacks the verbs and they all have the same subject, and the subject is God. He has cut down the might of Israel. He has burned like a flaming fire. He has bent his bow like an enemy. "He has bent his bow like an enemy, with his right hand set like a foe." (Lamentations 2:4) Job felt the same arrow. "I was at ease, and he broke me apart. He seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces. He set me up as his target." (Job 16:12) Isaiah would not soften it either. The people rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, "therefore he turned to be their enemy, and himself fought against them." (Isaiah 63:10) Here is what we want and cannot have. We want the disaster to come from somewhere outside of God's reach, so that we can run to God from it. Lamentations will not give us that exit. The hand that struck the city was not a foreign hand. He himself bent the bow.

And the poet will not let us file this under metaphor and move on. He pushes it through the whole sanctuary. "The Lord has scorned his altar, disowned his sanctuary. He has delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces." (Lamentations 2:7) His altar. His sanctuary. The God who commanded that the temple be built handed it over to the men who burned it. There is no comfort to be salvaged by pretending God was somewhere else when it happened, weeping helplessly on the sidelines while Babylon did what Babylon does. He was not on the sidelines. He gave the order. A smaller god would be easier to worship and impossible to trust, because a god who cannot touch your suffering cannot save you from it either. The poet would rather have the terrible God who is actually sovereign than the tame god who is merely absent.

**The sin underneath the silence**
Grant the hardest objection its full weight. If God did this, is God then cruel, a deity who delights in the ruin of children and the burning of his own house. The poet does not dodge that question. He answers it, but not by softening the blow — by naming the long provocation underneath it. The God of Israel was not a short-tempered tyrant looking for a reason. He was a patient covenant Lord whose people had spent generations treating his patience as permission. Jeremiah had told them their wound was the wound of a guilt that had grown numb. "Your guilt is great. Because your sins are flagrant, I have done these things to you." (Jeremiah 30:14) This is the discipline of a Father, and the New Testament will say it plainly. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives." (Hebrews 12:6) But — and the poet refuses to rush here — knowing it is discipline does not make it stop hurting, and Lamentations never pretends it does. The right answer to the doctrine of God's sovereign hand is not a shrug. It is a scream toward heaven. Truth that you cannot weep over is not truth you have actually received.

The poet models exactly this. He has just confessed that God did it, and in the very next breath his own body breaks. "My eyes are spent with weeping. My stomach churns. My bile is poured out to the ground because of the destruction of the daughter of my people." (Lamentations 2:11) This is the man who knows the doctrine is true, and the doctrine does not dry his eyes. It is precisely because he believes God's hand was in it that the grief goes all the way down. A pagan could shrug at a random catastrophe. Only a believer can be undone by one, because only a believer has to reckon with the fact that the God he loves is the God who allowed it. The doctrine does not numb the wound. It deepens it.

**Cry to him through the night about him**
So the poet teaches us the strangest prayer in Scripture. He teaches us to cry out to God about God. "Cry aloud to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears stream down like a torrent day and night. Give yourself no rest, your eyes no respite." (Lamentations 2:18) He does not say make peace with it. He does not say accept it. He says pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord — toward the very One whose hand did this. And this is the secret the comfortable believer never learns, because the comfortable believer has never been forced to. The opposite of faith is not anger at God. The opposite of faith is leaving the room. The poet stays in the room. He keeps his face toward the God who wounded him, and he weeps at him, and that staying is itself the deepest confession of trust in the whole Bible — I will not look anywhere else, even now, even when the wound is yours. I have counseled people to make peace with their grief, and I was wrong, because Lamentations does not make peace with it. It carries it straight to God and refuses to leave. And there is a darker night still, where another Son cried out toward the Father whose hand was on him. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me." (Matthew 27:46) The enemy's bow that bent against Jerusalem bent fully against Christ, and he absorbed it, so that the cry through the night would not be the last word. The God who became like an enemy to a guilty city became, in his Son, the friend of sinners by taking the bow into his own body.

He himself bent the bow.

## Great Is Your Faithfulness
*Hope found at the bottom, not at the exit*

**Text:** Lamentations 3:1-33 · **Supporting:** Job 13:15; Psalm 42:5; Micah 7:8; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9

The most quoted line in this book sits in the middle of the most hopeless chapter in this book, and we have spent decades singing the line while skipping the chapter. We put "great is your faithfulness" on the coffee mug. We leave off the forty verses of darkness it climbs out of. That is not how the poet wrote it, and the order matters more than almost anything else we could say about it.

**The man who has seen affliction**
The third poem does not begin with hope. It begins with a man at the absolute floor. "I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath. He has driven and brought me into darkness without any light." (Lamentations 3:1-2) Read what follows and do not flinch from it. He has made my flesh and skin waste away. He has walled me about so I cannot escape. He has made my chains heavy. "He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding. He turned aside my steps and tore me to pieces. He has made me desolate." (Lamentations 3:10-11) Twenty verses of a man describing God as the predator hunting him down. This is not a man who has not yet heard the good news. This is a man who knows God and is describing what it feels like to be under his rod, and the poet gives him every word of it before he gives him a single word of comfort. Job spoke from the same floor — "though he slay me, I will hope in him" (Job 13:15) — and notice that Job's hope did not require the slaying to stop. The hope of Lamentations is not the hope that the darkness has lifted. It is hope found while the darkness is still total.

And the man goes further down before he goes up. He says God has shut out his prayer. "Though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer." (Lamentations 3:8) This is the floor beneath the floor — not only the affliction, but the sense that the affliction cannot even be prayed about, that the heavens are brass and the cries are not getting through. Anyone who has sat by a hospital bed and felt their prayers fall back on them unanswered knows this verse from the inside. The poet does not censor it. He lets the man say that God has walled up his way with blocks of stone and made his paths crooked. He lets him say his endurance has perished and so has his hope from the LORD. Hope perished, and named as perished, recorded in the Word of God without apology. The Bible is not embarrassed by the believer who has run out of hope. It gives him a chapter.

**But this I call to mind**
Then comes the turn, and it is the most important hinge in the Old Testament, and it turns on a decision, not a feeling. "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope." (Lamentations 3:21) He does not say the situation changed. He does not say he felt better. He says he made himself remember something, and the remembering — not the relief — is what gave him hope. What does he call to mind. "The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases, his mercies never come to an end. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness." (Lamentations 3:22-23) The Hebrew under "steadfast love" is chesed — covenant loyalty, the love that is bound by promise and cannot be exhausted by your failure. And here is what the man at the bottom understands that the man on the mountaintop never has to. Mercies that are new every morning are mercies you need every morning, because the night before used them all up. This is not a sunny verse. It is a verse for people who have just barely survived the dark and have to do it again tomorrow. The psalmist preached to his own collapsing soul the same way — "why are you cast down, O my soul. Hope in God." (Psalm 42:5) Hope here is not a mood. It is an act of memory performed against the evidence, in the dark, by a man who has decided that God's character is more reliable than his own despair.

**The hope that holds you without lying to you**
Notice what this hope does not do. It does not cancel the grief. The man does not stop being the man who has seen affliction. The poet keeps him in the pit even after the great confession, and tells us why God can be trusted there. "For the Lord will not cast off forever, but, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love. For he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men." (Lamentations 3:31-33) He does not afflict from his heart. The discipline is real, but it is not where God's heart is. His heart is in the compassion, and the affliction is the strange work he does not delight in. I have offered people a hope that was really just a hurry — a verse handed across the room to end the crying, because the crying made me uncomfortable. That is not what the poet does. He sits in the pit and remembers out loud, and the remembering holds the man without lifting him out yet. Micah learned to say it in the dark. "When I fall, I shall rise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me." (Micah 7:8) And Paul mapped the same terrain — "afflicted in every way, but not crushed. Struck down, but not destroyed." (2 Corinthians 4:8-9) The mercies new every morning have a name and a face. He is the man of sorrows, the one acquainted with grief, who went down to the floor of this very pit so that no believer would ever be alone on it again. He did not skip the chapter. He lived it.

His mercies are new tomorrow.

## The Siege and the Famine
*Counting the cost in starving children, refusing every comfortable abstraction*

**Text:** Lamentations 4 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 28:53; Jeremiah 19:9; Obadiah 1:12; Galatians 6:7

We like our judgments at a comfortable altitude. We like to speak of the fall of nations the way historians do, with dates and causes and lessons drawn. The fourth poem of Lamentations drags the camera down to the gutter and forces us to look at what a siege actually does to a body, and it will not let us look away into theory.

**Gold that has lost its shine**
The poet starts with the children, and he starts by mourning what they have become. "How the gold has grown dim, how the pure gold is changed. The holy stones lie scattered at the head of every street." (Lamentations 4:1) He is not talking about jewelry. The next verse tells us. "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots." (Lamentations 4:2) The children were the gold. And now the gold has lost its shine — not because gold can tarnish, but because famine has reduced what was priceless to what is disposable. Then the poet does the thing we most want him not to do. He makes it concrete. "The tongue of the nursing infant sticks to the roof of its mouth for thirst. The children beg for food, but no one gives to them." (Lamentations 4:4) And worse, unsayably worse — "the hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children." (Lamentations 4:10) Moses had warned them, in the covenant curses, that a siege could drive a mother to this (Deuteronomy 28:53), and Jeremiah had said it would come true (Jeremiah 19:9). The poet refuses every abstraction because sin is never abstract when the bill comes due. We sin in concepts. We pay in bodies. And the poet makes us count the bodies one at a time.

He even draws a comparison we would never dare to draw. "Happier were the victims of the sword than the victims of hunger, who wasted away, pierced by lack of the fruits of the field." (Lamentations 4:9) Better to die quickly by the blade than slowly by the famine. The poet has done the unthinkable arithmetic of suffering, the kind that only the truly afflicted ever do, ranking their agonies, and he has found a grief so long and so grinding that a fast death starts to look like mercy. This is not a man reaching for effect. This is a man telling the exact truth about what slow ruin does to people, and refusing to make it more bearable for the comfortable reader than it was for the starving city. The God who inspired this book did not flinch from the gutter. Neither may we.

**Even the priests, even the kings**
Grant the objection a hearing — surely the leaders, the anointed, the men of God, were spared the worst of this. The poet answers that they were not, and that their fall was the heart of the catastrophe. "This was for the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in the midst of her the blood of the righteous." (Lamentations 4:13) The shepherds had blood on their hands, and so they stagger blind through the streets, so defiled with blood that no one dares touch their garments. The leadership did not escape the judgment. The leadership was the reason for it. And the poet names the bitterest blow of all — "the LORD's anointed, the breath of our nostrils, was captured in their pits." (Lamentations 4:20) The king they had trusted to be their very breath, their life, is taken. The thing they organized their security around is gone. This is what judgment does. It comes for the idols first, and the leaders we trusted to keep us safe are very often the idols. A man reaps what he sows, and so does a nation, and so does a church (Galatians 6:7). I have stood in pulpits and trusted the structure to protect me, the position to keep me, and I have called that stewardship when it was hiding. We do this. We build our security on the breath of our own nostrils and call it faithfulness. We trust the king, the budget, the building, the reputation, the man at the top — and we call that wisdom right up until the day it is captured in the enemy's pit and we discover it could never have saved us at all.

**Not the final word over the enemy either**
Here the poem makes its hardest turn, and it is a turn toward justice, not toward despair. The judgment on God's people is terrible — and it is not the final word over those who gloated while it happened. "Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom. But to you also the cup shall pass. You shall become drunk and strip yourself bare." (Lamentations 4:21) Edom stood at the crossing and cheered while her brother bled, and Obadiah had said it plainly — do not gloat over the day of your brother's ruin (Obadiah 1:12). The God who disciplined his own children has not gone deaf to the cruelty of the ones who enjoyed it. And to the daughter of Zion, sitting in the ash and the famine, the poet says the thing that holds her up. "The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished. He will keep you in exile no longer." (Lamentations 4:22) Accomplished. The bill, terrible as it was, has an end. And the gospel takes that word and presses it to its limit, because there was a cup that was not passed but drunk, by the only innocent man, to the dregs. The man of sorrows took the famine of God-forsakenness so that the starving children of God would be fed. The cup passed to Edom because it had already been emptied by Christ. Even gold loses its shine — but he became poor, that we who were earthen pots might be made precious again.

Even gold loses its shine.

## Restore Us to Yourself
*The broken prayer with no guarantee, cast on the only throne that lasts*

**Text:** Lamentations 5 · **Supporting:** Nehemiah 9:16-17; Psalm 90:1-2; Daniel 9:8-9; Hebrews 13:8

The whole book has been built on a strict structure, four poems each marching through the Hebrew alphabet, grief organized line by ordered line. And then the final chapter breaks the form. It still has twenty-two verses, one for each letter, but the acrostic collapses. The order is gone. Because by the end, even the structure cannot hold the grief, and the people stop performing their lament and simply pray.

**Remember, O LORD**
The last poem opens not with poetry but with a plain plea. "Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us. Look, and see our disgrace." (Lamentations 5:1) And then the inventory, blunt and unadorned — our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, we have become orphans, fatherless, we pay for the water we drink, we are hunted, slaves rule over us, and there is no one to deliver us from their hand. "The joy of our hearts has ceased. Our dancing has been turned to mourning." (Lamentations 5:15) No metaphor here, no carried image. Just the list of what was lost, laid before God the way you would lay your hands open and empty on a table. This is the prayer of people too tired to be eloquent. And there is a kind of honesty available at the end of strength that is not available at the beginning, when we still have the energy to dress the grief up.

The poet lets the exhaustion show in the body of the prayer. "Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine." "The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music." "For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim." (Lamentations 5:10, 14, 17) The gate where elders once gave counsel sits empty. The music has stopped. Even the eyes, worn out from weeping, can barely see. This is what a whole community looks like when it has cried until there is nothing left, and the prayer does not pretend otherwise. It does not summon a false strength to impress God. It comes empty, and empty is where this kind of prayer has to start.

**The sin of the fathers and the sin of us**
Then the community does the thing that makes this prayer trustworthy. It confesses, and it confesses without flinching from its own generation's part. "Our fathers sinned, and are no more, and we bear their iniquities." (Lamentations 5:7) That alone could be a complaint — we are paying for what they did. But the poet will not let the prayer stop at blaming the dead. Three verses from the end, the confession turns inward and present. "Woe to us, for we have sinned." (Lamentations 5:16) Not only them. Us. Both are true and the prayer holds both — the inheritance of sin we did not choose, and the sin we ourselves committed, and it confesses both without using one to excuse the other. Daniel would pray this exact prayer in exile — "to us belongs open shame, but to the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness" (Daniel 9:8-9). Nehemiah's people would stand and confess the same long arc — that their fathers acted presumptuously, and yet God was ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger (Nehemiah 9:16-17). I have been quick to bear my fathers' iniquities as a grievance and slow to confess my own as a sin. We do this. We inherit the wound and we add to it, and we want credit for the first while hiding the second. The fatherless man knows this temptation better than most, the pull to make the whole of your brokenness somebody else's fault, to point at the absence that shaped you and stop the accounting there. The prayer will not stop there. It bears the fathers' iniquity and confesses its own, and it does both in the same breath, because that is what honest grief before God finally sounds like.

**The throne that does not fall, and the prayer with no guarantee**
And then, at the bottom of everything, with the city gone and the structure broken and the future blank, the prayer reaches for the one thing that has not changed. "But you, O LORD, reign forever. Your throne endures to all generations." (Lamentations 5:19) Everything else has fallen. The temple, the kingship, the land, the dancing. The throne of the LORD has not. Moses had prayed it before there was a Jerusalem to lose — "Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. From everlasting to everlasting you are God." (Psalm 90:1-2) The same God, yesterday and today and forever (Hebrews 13:8). On that throne, and on nothing else, the people cast their whole future in the last words of the book. "Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored. Renew our days as of old — unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us." (Lamentations 5:21-22) And the book ends there. On a plea, and a fear. Not on a promise of yes. The Hebrew leaves the door open and refuses to close it for us, and we must sit with the fact that the inspired word of God ends the book of grief without telling the griever the answer is coming. That unresolved ending is not a failure of faith. It is the truest faith there is — casting yourself on a God who has every right to reject you, with no guarantee in your hand except his eternal reign. We who read it from this side of the cross know that the restoration came, that the man of sorrows was raised, that the throne that endures forever has a Lamb on it. But the people who prayed this did not know. They prayed anyway. And the God enthroned forever did not, in the end, reject them. He sent his Son into their grief to bring them home.

Restore us, unless you have rejected us.
